forecasts.label: Capital expenditure

news_drafts.headline: Derby Cabinet papers put Waste Treatment Centre write-down at about £51.4m, with government permission sought
news_drafts.lead:
Derby City Council expects to write down the value of the Derby and Derbyshire Waste Treatment Centre by about £51.407m after deciding not to operate the facility, according to the Medium Term Financial Strategy paper before its Cabinet on 7 October 2026. The council's chief finance officer is required to ask government for a capitalisation direction (permission to treat day-to-day spending as if it were capital spending, so it can be paid for by borrowing or asset sales).

The paper describes the figure as an impairment and write-back, which is an accounting entry recording that the plant will no longer produce the benefits the council had expected from it. It says this is not a new cash cost. The paper puts the council's current estimate at "approximately £51.407m" and says the scale of the effect is why the direction is needed, to manage what it means for the council's day-to-day budget (revenue spending).

The paper is part of the council's medium-term financial strategy, its financial plan for the next few years. The material available to this desk does not give the timetable for the government's decision, nor how the council would cover the sum if permission were granted.

news_drafts.headline: Derby's borrowing need reaches £934m as capital programme drives rise in debt financing costs
news_drafts.lead: Derby City Council's capital financing requirement — the total of long-lived assets it has funded that it has not yet paid for — reached £933.704m in the first quarter of the financial year, up £58.9m from the previous March. The rise reflects the council's substantial capital programme of £226.3m for 2026/27, led by the Our City Our River project at £78.4m and schools building work at £73m, alongside new accounting rules requiring lease liabilities to be shown on the balance sheet. The council's treasury management report to its Audit and Governance Committee forecasts it will need to borrow £439.9m in new external loans by 2032 as internal reserves decline from £313.2m to £157.6m. Financing costs — interest and repayments on borrowing — are forecast to rise from £23.4m in the current year to £38.7m by 2028/29, consuming 9 per cent of the net revenue stream by then, up from 7 per cent now. The council's net borrowing position fell by £20.6m in the quarter to £451.2m, reflecting timing of grant and tax receipts rather than debt reduction.

findings.paper_title: Item 16 - Contract and Financial Procedure Matters
findings.headline: Infinity Park Enterprise Zone business rates (£0.646m in 2026/27, forecast £0.777m in 2027/28) retained by Derby through 31 March 2041, moving from EMCCA passporting to direct council management.
findings.detail: Derby is taking direct ownership of business rates generated within the Infinity Park Enterprise Zone, with forecasts of £0.646m in 2026/27 and £0.777m in 2027/28, continuing through March 2041. A new reserve 'IPD Retained Business Rates' will manage these funds; 2026/27 expenditure is planned at £0.372m for existing commitments and £0.274m for feasibility works on pipeline projects (Infinity HQ, Technology Hub, power infrastructure), with any surplus retained in reserve.
findings.matters: Councils securing long-term ring-fenced revenue streams from strategic regeneration sites demonstrate how they fund capital infrastructure investment. For lenders, this shows tangible revenue sources supporting capital commitments. For peer councils, this illustrates governance structures for managing designated zone revenues.
findings.figures: Business rates income £0.646m in 2026/27, forecast £0.777m in 2027/28, policy active until 31 March 2041, feasibility work allocation up to £0.500m
findings.quote: Participation in the EZ and designation of a BRR site provides the opportunity for the Council to secure and re-invest 100% of IPD business rates generated until March 2041.

findings.paper_title: Item 16 - Contract and Financial Procedure Matters
findings.headline: Morleston Short Break Centre capital scheme increases from £2.638m to £3.322m with project redirected from refurbishment to demolition and new build.
findings.detail: The scheme for relocating the Bonsall View short breaks service (approved January 2026) has been fundamentally redirected. The original budget of £2.638m for refurbishment has become £3.322m for demolition and new build, an increase of £0.684m (26%). The change follows assessment that the existing building is unsuitable for long-term service delivery due to condition, layout and structural limitations. Capital costs of £0.085m incurred on the original refurbishment proposal have been written off as abortive. The revised budget is profiled £0.671m in 2026/27 and £2.651m in 2027/28, to be funded from existing property budgets.
findings.matters: Councils and lenders track capital project escalations and mid-project redirects as indicators of execution risk. A scheme approved less than a year ago now requires a 26% budget increase and fundamental change of approach, signalling either inadequate initial assessment or unforeseen conditions that other councils managing similar projects will want to monitor.
findings.figures: Original budget £2.638m, revised budget £3.322m, increase £0.684m (26%), abortive costs £0.085m
findings.quote: Capital costs of £0.085m incurred in relation to the original refurbishment proposal have been identified as abortive following the decision (if approved) to proceed with the alternative scheme (demolition and new build).

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: Council tax increase 4.99% to £1,898.99 Band D, at maximum allowable rate
findings.detail: Derby is applying a 4.99% council tax increase for 2026/27, raising Band D to £1,898.99. This is at the maximum permitted level and matches Leicester. Nottingham is increasing at 3.5% and Coventry at 3.9%. The council notes that government core spending calculations assume councils maximise tax levies, so accepting less than 4.99% would reduce spending power further.
findings.matters: A council at maximum tax increases signals constraint by legislation rather than restraint. This typically precedes requests to government for additional flexibility or funding and indicates limited scope to raise revenue locally.
findings.figures: Council tax increase 4.99%, Band D £1,898.99; Leicester 4.99%; Nottingham 3.5%; Coventry 3.9%
findings.quote: Government core spending calculations are based on council's maximising their council tax levies so by not applying the maximum council tax increase allowable it will not see the maximum real terms increase in spending power, this will limit its ability to fund essential services

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: £7.105m permanent budget savings required in 2026/27 with delivery risk flagged
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget requires delivery of £7.105m permanent savings to achieve balance. The council flags this as a material risk: 'The risk of not delivering these savings is being monitored and reported to Cabinet. Risk within these plans must be mitigated by directors owning and delivering their savings commitments or identifying alternative delivery savings.' This continues a pattern of large annual savings dependency; since 2010/11 the council has delivered £261m cumulative savings.
findings.matters: Councils dependent on ongoing large savings delivery face execution risk; failure to deliver can quickly create deficits. The fact that such savings are flagged as a material risk suggests confidence in full delivery is not complete.
findings.figures: Required permanent savings 2026/27 £7.105m; cumulative savings since 2010/11 £261m
findings.quote: the budget for 2026/27 required permanent budget savings of £7.105m to be delivered to bring the budget into balance. The risk of not delivering these savings is being monitored and reported to Cabinet

findings.paper_title: Item 14 - Medium Term Financial Strategy including National Issues and Derby Focus
findings.headline: Capital programme increased to £227.272m with 29% (c.£66m) funded by unsupported borrowing
findings.detail: The capital programme forecast has increased from £220.538m approved to £227.272m at Q1 2026/27. Funding sources: 53% Government Grants (c.£120m), 29% Unsupported Borrowing (c.£66m), 6% Capital Receipts, 7% Major Repairs Allowance, with minor contributions from reserves, direct revenue, Section 106 and external contributions. The council notes that 'the future capital programme will continue to be reviewed to reduce the forecast level of borrowing', indicating concern at current unsupported borrowing levels and their revenue impact.
findings.matters: Capital programme growth funded by increased borrowing shifts risk onto the revenue budget through debt servicing. A council signalling intent to reduce borrowing is making an explicit tradeoff between capital ambitions and revenue sustainability.
findings.figures: Capital programme Q1 2026/27 forecast £227.272m; Unsupported Borrowing 29% (c.£66m); Government Grants 53% (c.£120m)
findings.quote: The capital expenditure forecast as at Qtr. 1 is £227.272m...The future capital programme will continue to be reviewed to reduce the forecast level of borrowing and maintain an affordable and sustainable capital programme
